question: In Arizona, a real estate agency relationship between a broker and a client is most commonly created by which of the following?
choice_a: Simply showing a property to a member of the public
choice_b: A written listing agreement or buyer-broker agreement signed by the client and the broker (or the broker's licensee)
choice_c: Automatically, the moment a salesperson obtains a real estate license
choice_d: Verbal agreement only, since Arizona does not allow written agency agreements
explanation: Arizona agency relationships in real estate are established by a written employment agreement between the client (seller or buyer) and the broker, such as a listing agreement or buyer-broker agreement. Casual contact, such as showing a home to the public, does not by itself create an agency relationship.
source_note: A.R.S. Title 32, Chapter 20 (Real Estate); Arizona Department of Real Estate licensee duties framework

question: Under Arizona real estate practice, which agency relationship allows one licensee in a firm to represent the seller and a different licensee in the same firm to represent the buyer, each owing full fiduciary duties only to their own client?
choice_a: Dual agency
choice_b: Subagency
choice_c: Designated agency
choice_d: Transaction brokerage with no client representation
explanation: Designated agency allows the employing broker to appoint one licensee to represent the seller and another licensee within the same brokerage to represent the buyer. Each designated agent owes full fiduciary duties to their own client, unlike dual agency where a single licensee represents both parties.
source_note: Arizona Department of Real Estate licensee agency-relationship framework; A.R.S. Title 32, Chapter 20

question: Before a single Arizona licensee may act as a dual agent representing both the buyer and seller in the same transaction, what must occur?
choice_a: Only the buyer needs to give verbal consent
choice_b: The Arizona Department of Real Estate must approve the transaction in advance
choice_c: Dual agency is prohibited outright in Arizona under all circumstances
choice_d: Both parties must give informed written consent to the dual agency after full disclosure
explanation: Arizona permits dual agency only when both the buyer and seller receive full disclosure of the dual role and give informed, written consent. Without that consent, a licensee may not act for both parties in the same transaction.
source_note: Arizona Department of Real Estate agency-disclosure and dual agency framework, A.R.S. Title 32, Chapter 20

question: A licensee who assists a buyer or seller but does not represent either party as a fiduciary, instead facilitating the transaction in a limited, non-agency capacity, is best described in Arizona practice as a
choice_a: Transaction broker / limited representative
choice_b: General agent
choice_c: Universal agent
choice_d: Subagent of the seller
explanation: A transaction broker or limited representative facilitates a real estate transaction without forming a full fiduciary agency relationship with either party, distinguishing this role from single agency, dual agency, or designated agency, all of which involve fiduciary representation.
source_note: Arizona Department of Real Estate agency-relationship framework

question: Which type of listing agreement gives an Arizona seller's broker the right to a commission regardless of who ultimately procures the buyer, including the seller?
choice_a: Open listing
choice_b: Exclusive right to sell listing
choice_c: Exclusive agency listing
choice_d: Net listing (as typically discouraged)
explanation: An exclusive right to sell listing entitles the listing broker to a commission no matter who finds the buyer, including the seller acting alone. This differs from an exclusive agency listing, under which the seller retains the right to sell without owing a commission if the seller personally procures the buyer.
source_note: General Arizona real estate listing-agreement practice, A.R.S. Title 32, Chapter 20

question: Under an exclusive agency listing in Arizona, in what specific circumstance does the seller NOT owe the listing broker a commission?
choice_a: When any licensed broker other than the listing broker procures the buyer
choice_b: When the listing broker itself procures the buyer
choice_c: When the seller personally finds and sells to a buyer without any broker's assistance
choice_d: Under no circumstance -- a commission is always owed
explanation: An exclusive agency listing reserves the seller's right to sell the property without paying a commission only if the seller, without any broker involvement, personally procures the buyer. If any broker (including a cooperating broker) is involved, a commission is generally owed.
source_note: General Arizona real estate listing-agreement practice

question: In an open listing arrangement, how many brokers may a seller simultaneously engage to market the same property?
choice_a: Exactly one broker, who is guaranteed the commission
choice_b: None -- open listings are illegal in Arizona
choice_c: Two brokers only, split evenly regardless of who sells the property
choice_d: Multiple brokers, with commission owed only to the one who successfully procures a buyer
explanation: An open listing is non-exclusive, allowing a seller to list the same property with multiple brokers at once. Only the broker who actually procures a ready, willing, and able buyer earns the commission; the others earn nothing.
source_note: General Arizona real estate listing-agreement practice

question: A buyer-broker agreement in Arizona primarily serves to
choice_a: Establish an agency relationship in which the broker represents the buyer's interests and defines the broker's compensation
choice_b: Transfer title of the property to the buyer
choice_c: Waive the buyer's right to any property inspection
choice_d: Automatically make the buyer's broker a subagent of the seller
explanation: A buyer-broker (buyer representation) agreement creates an agency relationship in which the broker owes fiduciary duties to the buyer as client and spells out how and when the broker will be compensated, replacing older practices where cooperating brokers automatically acted as subagents of the seller.
source_note: Arizona Department of Real Estate buyer representation practice, A.R.S. Title 32, Chapter 20

question: Which of the following is required content typically found in an Arizona exclusive buyer-broker or listing agreement?
choice_a: A guarantee that the property will sell at listed price
choice_b: A definite termination date
choice_c: A waiver of the client's right to cancel under any circumstance
choice_d: A clause making the agreement perpetual with no end date
explanation: Arizona listing and buyer-broker agreements must contain a definite termination date; open-ended or perpetual agency agreements without an expiration are not permitted under Arizona real estate licensing standards.
source_note: Arizona Department of Real Estate contract-content requirements, A.R.S. Title 32, Chapter 20

question: An Arizona real estate agency relationship, once properly formed under a listing or buyer-broker agreement, obligates the broker to act primarily in whose interest?
choice_a: The broker's own financial interest above all others
choice_b: Whichever party pays the commission, regardless of who is the client
choice_c: The client (the principal) who engaged the broker
choice_d: The cooperating broker on the other side of the transaction
explanation: Once an agency relationship is created, the broker's fiduciary obligation runs to the client (principal), not automatically to whoever pays the commission. A seller's broker, for example, still owes fiduciary duties to the seller even though the buyer's proceeds may ultimately fund the commission.
source_note: General agency law principles applied to Arizona real estate practice

question: Which best describes a 'customer' as distinguished from a 'client' in Arizona real estate agency terminology?
choice_a: A customer is another term for the licensee's own broker
choice_b: A customer always has an exclusive agency agreement with the licensee
choice_c: There is no legal distinction between a customer and a client in Arizona
choice_d: A customer is a party to the transaction to whom the licensee owes duties of honesty and fair dealing but not full fiduciary duties
explanation: In Arizona agency terminology, a 'client' is a party represented under an agency agreement and owed full fiduciary duties, while a 'customer' is the other party in the transaction, to whom the licensee still owes honesty, fair dealing, and disclosure of material facts, but not fiduciary loyalty or confidentiality.
source_note: Arizona Department of Real Estate licensee duties framework

question: A seller's agent in Arizona is showing the property to a prospective buyer who is unrepresented. What duty does the seller's agent still owe to that unrepresented buyer?
choice_a: Honesty and fair dealing, including disclosure of known material facts about the property
choice_b: The same fiduciary loyalty and confidentiality owed to the seller
choice_c: No duty whatsoever, since the buyer is not the agent's client
choice_d: A duty to negotiate the lowest possible price on the buyer's behalf
explanation: Even when representing only the seller, an Arizona licensee owes any unrepresented buyer basic duties of honesty, fair dealing, and disclosure of known material facts, while fiduciary duties such as loyalty and confidentiality remain owed exclusively to the seller-client.
source_note: Arizona Department of Real Estate licensee duties to clients and customers framework

question: Which statement correctly distinguishes 'designated agency' from 'dual agency' in Arizona?
choice_a: Designated agency and dual agency are the same thing under Arizona law
choice_b: Designated agency assigns separate licensees within the same firm to each party, while dual agency has one licensee representing both parties
choice_c: Designated agency is illegal in Arizona, while dual agency is required in every in-house sale
choice_d: Designated agency only applies to commercial property; dual agency only applies to residential property
explanation: Designated agency separates representation between two different licensees within the same brokerage, each advocating solely for their own client, whereas dual agency involves a single licensee attempting to represent both parties simultaneously with divided loyalty, requiring informed written consent.
source_note: Arizona Department of Real Estate agency-relationship framework

question: When must an Arizona real estate licensee first disclose in writing which party or parties they represent in a transaction?
choice_a: Only after closing has occurred
choice_b: Disclosure of agency is optional in Arizona
choice_c: At the earliest practicable opportunity in the transaction, before eliciting confidential information
choice_d: Only if directly asked by the other party
explanation: Arizona licensees are expected to disclose their agency status early in dealings with the public, before confidential information might be shared, so that all parties understand who the licensee represents and can act accordingly.
source_note: Arizona Department of Real Estate agency-disclosure framework, A.R.S. Title 32, Chapter 20

question: A buyer tells their Arizona buyer's agent, in confidence, that they would be willing to pay more than their current offer if needed. Under fiduciary duty, what must the agent do with that information?
choice_a: Immediately relay it to the seller's agent to speed up negotiations
choice_b: Disclose it to the Arizona Department of Real Estate
choice_c: Share it with other prospective buyers to gauge market interest
choice_d: Keep it confidential and not disclose it to the seller or seller's agent without the buyer's permission
explanation: The fiduciary duty of confidentiality requires a buyer's agent to protect a client's confidential negotiating information, including willingness to pay more, unless the client authorizes its release. Disclosing it to the other side would breach that duty and harm the client's negotiating position.
source_note: Arizona fiduciary duty of confidentiality (part of the 'OLDCAR' duties framework)

question: The fiduciary duties an Arizona real estate licensee owes a client are often summarized by the mnemonic 'OLDCAR.' What does the 'O' stand for?
choice_a: Obedience -- following the client's lawful instructions
choice_b: Openness -- disclosing everything to all parties equally
choice_c: Ownership -- holding title on the client's behalf
choice_d: Origination -- generating new leads for the client
explanation: In the OLDCAR mnemonic, 'O' stands for Obedience: the duty to follow the client's lawful instructions. The full set is Obedience, Loyalty, Disclosure, Confidentiality, Accounting, and Reasonable care/diligence.
source_note: Common fiduciary-duties mnemonic taught in Arizona real estate licensing courses

question: Which fiduciary duty requires an Arizona licensee to properly handle and account for all client funds, such as earnest money deposits, and never commingle them with personal funds?
choice_a: Obedience
choice_b: Accounting
choice_c: Loyalty
choice_d: Disclosure
explanation: The fiduciary duty of accounting obligates the licensee to properly track, safeguard, and report on all money and property entrusted to them by a client, including avoiding commingling of client funds with personal or brokerage operating funds.
source_note: Arizona fiduciary duty of accounting; A.R.S. Title 32, Chapter 20 trust fund handling provisions

question: The fiduciary duty of loyalty owed by an Arizona licensee to their client means the agent must
choice_a: Always agree with everything the client says, even if unlawful
choice_b: Represent the opposing party equally in the same transaction
choice_c: Place the client's interests above the agent's own personal or financial interests in the transaction
choice_d: Prioritize a quick closing over the client's stated goals
explanation: Loyalty requires the agent to act in the client's best interest, avoiding self-dealing or conflicts of interest, such as secretly profiting from the transaction at the client's expense.
source_note: Arizona fiduciary duty of loyalty (OLDCAR framework)

question: The fiduciary duty of reasonable care and skill requires an Arizona licensee to
choice_a: Guarantee a specific sale price for the client
choice_b: Provide legal advice in place of an attorney whenever asked
choice_c: Waive any duty of competence when the client is experienced
choice_d: Perform the tasks of the agency with the competence expected of a reasonably prudent real estate professional
explanation: The duty of reasonable care and skill requires the licensee to perform agency responsibilities -- pricing guidance, marketing, negotiation, disclosure review -- with the level of competence a reasonably prudent licensee would exercise, without overstepping into unlicensed practices such as giving legal advice.
source_note: Arizona fiduciary duty of reasonable care (OLDCAR framework)

question: Which of the following would most clearly violate an Arizona listing agent's fiduciary duty of disclosure to their seller-client?
choice_a: Failing to tell the seller about a written offer received from a buyer
choice_b: Telling the seller the property received a full-price offer
choice_c: Advising the seller to consult an attorney about a contract clause
choice_d: Recommending the seller obtain a pre-listing inspection
explanation: The fiduciary duty of disclosure requires the agent to promptly communicate all relevant information -- including any written offer -- to the client. Withholding a received offer from the seller is a serious breach of that duty.
source_note: Arizona fiduciary duty of disclosure (OLDCAR framework)

question: A dual agent in Arizona who has obtained informed written consent from both parties must still be especially careful about which fiduciary duty, since it becomes limited by the dual role?
choice_a: Accounting for trust funds, which no longer applies in dual agency
choice_b: Full, undivided loyalty to either party, since loyalty must now be balanced between both clients
choice_c: Obedience, which is eliminated entirely in dual agency
choice_d: Duty to cooperate with other brokers, which becomes mandatory only in dual agency
explanation: In dual agency, the licensee cannot provide full, undivided loyalty to one party without disadvantaging the other, so that duty is necessarily limited and balanced between both clients. This is precisely why informed written consent is required before dual agency may proceed.
source_note: Arizona Department of Real Estate dual agency limitations framework

question: In Arizona, every actively licensed real estate salesperson and associate broker must be supervised by which of the following?
choice_a: Any licensed salesperson willing to volunteer as a mentor
choice_b: The Arizona Department of Real Estate directly, without any brokerage-level supervision
choice_c: A designated (employing) broker who holds an active broker's license
choice_d: No supervision is required once a salesperson passes the state exam
explanation: Arizona law requires every salesperson and associate broker to work under the supervision of a designated (employing) broker, who is responsible for the actions of licensees within the brokerage.
source_note: A.R.S. Section 32-2155 (restriction on employment of a person as broker or salesperson) and related designated-broker supervision requirements, A.R.S. Title 32, Chapter 20

question: Under Arizona real estate law, a designated broker's duty to 'exercise reasonable supervision' over licensees in the brokerage extends to which of the following?
choice_a: Only fully licensed associate brokers, never salespersons
choice_b: Only licensees who have been disciplined previously
choice_c: No one, since supervision is solely the Department's responsibility
choice_d: Even exempt residential leasing agents or property managers working under the brokerage
explanation: Arizona statute makes clear that even when certain residential leasing agents or property managers are exempt from licensure requirements, the designated broker is still responsible for exercising reasonable supervision over them, underscoring how broad the designated broker's oversight duty is.
source_note: A.R.S. Section 32-2155(E), designated broker supervisory responsibility over exempt leasing agents/managers

question: Failing to reasonably supervise licensees affiliated with the brokerage can subject an Arizona designated broker to which consequence?
choice_a: Disciplinary action by the Arizona Department of Real Estate, potentially including suspension or revocation of the broker's license
choice_b: No consequence at all, since only the individual salesperson can be disciplined
choice_c: Automatic criminal prosecution with no administrative process
choice_d: Only a small civil fine paid directly to the salesperson
explanation: The Arizona Department of Real Estate Commissioner may deny, suspend, or revoke a designated broker's license for failing to reasonably supervise licensees under the broker's employ, since responsible supervision is a core statutory duty of the designated broker role.
source_note: A.R.S. Section 32-2153 (grounds for denial, suspension or revocation of licenses) as applied to designated broker supervisory failures

question: In the Arizona brokerage structure, who is legally accountable to the Arizona Department of Real Estate for the licensed activities of salespersons and associate brokers in the firm?
choice_a: Each individual salesperson, entirely independent of the firm
choice_b: The designated broker of the firm
choice_c: The buyer or seller involved in each transaction
choice_d: The escrow agent handling the closing
explanation: The designated broker is the licensee legally responsible to the Department for the brokerage's operations and the conduct of its affiliated salespersons and associate brokers, forming the backbone of Arizona's broker-supervision structure.
source_note: A.R.S. Title 32, Chapter 20, designated broker responsibility structure

question: May an Arizona salesperson be employed by or receive compensation from more than one designated broker at the same time for real estate activity?
choice_a: Yes, without any restriction
choice_b: Yes, but only for commercial transactions
choice_c: No -- a salesperson may be licensed under only one designated broker at a time
choice_d: Yes, provided the salesperson notifies the buyer verbally
explanation: Arizona restricts a salesperson's real estate compensation and licensure to a single designated broker at a time, reinforcing the clear line of supervisory accountability the designated-broker system is meant to create.
source_note: A.R.S. Section 32-2155, restriction on employment or compensation of a salesperson

question: What is the primary purpose of Arizona's requirement that every real estate office operate under a designated broker?
choice_a: To guarantee the office generates a minimum number of annual sales
choice_b: To allow the office to bypass state advertising rules
choice_c: To eliminate the need for individual salesperson licensing
choice_d: To ensure a single, accountable, licensed individual actively supervises licensee conduct and compliance at that office
explanation: The designated broker requirement exists to place clear supervisory and compliance responsibility with one licensed, accountable individual at each brokerage location, protecting consumers and maintaining professional standards.
source_note: A.R.S. Title 32, Chapter 20, designated broker framework

question: A salesperson's commission check for a completed sale in Arizona must, as a matter of proper brokerage practice, be paid
choice_a: Through the salesperson's designated broker, not directly from the buyer, seller, or another licensee
choice_b: Directly by the buyer to the salesperson in cash
choice_c: Directly by any cooperating broker to the salesperson, bypassing the salesperson's own broker
choice_d: Only after the Arizona Department of Real Estate personally approves the amount
explanation: Because a salesperson may only be compensated through their designated broker, commission funds must flow through that broker rather than coming directly from a client or another firm, preserving the broker's supervisory and accounting responsibility.
source_note: A.R.S. Section 32-2155, restriction on compensation of salespersons outside the designated broker relationship

question: If an Arizona associate broker wants to supervise other licensees directly the way a designated broker does, what must first occur?
choice_a: Nothing -- all associate brokers automatically have full supervisory authority
choice_b: The associate broker must be appointed or function as the designated broker (or a delegated supervising broker) for that office
choice_c: The associate broker must first become a salesperson again
choice_d: Supervisory authority is granted the moment the broker's exam is passed, with no appointment needed
explanation: Holding an associate broker's license alone does not confer designated-broker supervisory authority; that authority attaches to the specific role of designated broker (or a properly delegated branch/supervising broker) for the office in question.
source_note: A.R.S. Title 32, Chapter 20, distinction between associate broker licensure and designated broker role

question: Which best explains why Arizona's designated-broker supervision requirement is considered central to consumer protection in real estate transactions?
choice_a: It removes any state oversight because supervision is entirely delegated to the private sector
choice_b: It guarantees that no consumer complaint will ever be filed against the brokerage
choice_c: It creates a single, licensed point of accountability who can be disciplined for the misconduct of licensees under their supervision, encouraging active oversight
choice_d: It allows salespersons to operate completely independently without any accountability
explanation: By making one licensed, accountable individual (the designated broker) responsible for supervising all licensee conduct at a firm, Arizona creates strong incentives for brokers to actively monitor transactions, training, and compliance, which protects consumers from unsupervised misconduct.
source_note: A.R.S. Title 32, Chapter 20, designated-broker accountability framework

question: A seller signs an exclusive right to sell listing agreement with an Arizona broker but later sells the home to a family member without any broker involvement before the listing expires. What is the likely result?
choice_a: No commission is owed because family sales are always exempt
choice_b: The seller automatically forfeits ownership of the property
choice_c: The listing agreement is voided the moment any family member is involved
choice_d: The listing broker may still be owed the agreed commission because the exclusive right to sell entitles the broker to compensation regardless of who procures the buyer
explanation: Because an exclusive right to sell listing entitles the broker to a commission no matter who produces the buyer -- including the seller personally -- selling to a family member during the listing term would typically still trigger the broker's right to commission under the agreement's terms.
source_note: General Arizona exclusive right to sell listing practice

question: Which of the following is an accurate statement about subagency in modern Arizona real estate practice?
choice_a: Subagency, once common through cooperating MLS brokers automatically representing the seller, has been largely replaced by buyer representation and designated agency models
choice_b: Subagency is the only lawful agency relationship recognized in Arizona today
choice_c: A subagent owes fiduciary duties exclusively to the buyer
choice_d: Subagency eliminates the need for any agency disclosure
explanation: Historically, cooperating brokers who showed a seller's listed property were treated as subagents of the seller, owing the seller fiduciary duties even though they worked with the buyer. Modern practice has shifted heavily toward buyer representation and designated agency, making pure subagency far less common.
source_note: Arizona Department of Real Estate agency-relationship evolution framework

question: An Arizona buyer's agent learns the seller is in serious financial distress and might accept significantly less than the asking price. What does the fiduciary duty of confidentiality (owed to the buyer) permit the agent to do with the buyer's own bargaining strategy information?
choice_a: The agent must disclose the buyer's maximum offer price directly to the seller as a courtesy
choice_b: The agent may use the seller's distress information in negotiating for the buyer, since that information was learned about the customer (seller), not confidential client information that must be protected from the other side
choice_c: The agent must refuse to represent the buyer once financial distress is discovered
choice_d: The agent must report the seller's financial distress to the Arizona Department of Real Estate
explanation: Confidentiality duties run to the agent's own client. Information learned about the other side (here, the seller's financial distress) is not the buyer's confidential information and can generally be used in negotiation for the buyer's benefit, so long as no fiduciary or legal duty to the seller as a customer, such as honesty, is violated.
source_note: Arizona fiduciary duty of confidentiality, applied to client vs. customer information

question: Which scenario best illustrates a breach of the fiduciary duty of obedience by an Arizona listing agent?
choice_a: The agent presents every written offer to the seller promptly, as instructed
choice_b: The agent declines to help the seller violate fair housing law even though instructed to do so
choice_c: The agent refuses the seller's lawful instruction to present all offers within 24 hours, instead delaying disclosure of a competing offer for a week
choice_d: The agent follows the seller's lawful request to hold open houses only on weekends
explanation: Obedience requires the agent to follow the client's lawful instructions. Ignoring a lawful, reasonable instruction (like promptly presenting offers) breaches that duty. Note that obedience never requires following an unlawful instruction, such as one that would violate fair housing law.
source_note: Arizona fiduciary duty of obedience (OLDCAR framework), limited to lawful instructions

question: In Arizona, does the fiduciary duty of obedience require a licensee to follow a client's instruction to discriminate against a prospective buyer based on a protected class?
choice_a: Yes -- the client's instructions must always be followed without exception
choice_b: Yes, but only if the client puts the instruction in writing
choice_c: The duty of obedience overrides all other state and federal law
choice_d: No -- obedience only extends to lawful instructions, and discrimination would violate fair housing law
explanation: The fiduciary duty of obedience is limited to lawful instructions. A licensee must never follow a client's instruction that would violate the law, such as engaging in discriminatory practices prohibited by fair housing law, regardless of the client's wishes.
source_note: Arizona fiduciary duty of obedience, limited by legal compliance obligations including federal Fair Housing Act

question: An Arizona brokerage terminates its relationship with a salesperson. What must happen to that salesperson's license status with the Arizona Department of Real Estate?
choice_a: The designated broker must notify the Department, and the salesperson cannot conduct licensed activity until re-affiliated with a new designated broker
choice_b: Nothing changes -- the salesperson may continue working independently without a broker
choice_c: The salesperson automatically becomes the new designated broker
choice_d: The salesperson's license converts automatically to a broker's license
explanation: Because Arizona salespersons must be affiliated with and supervised by a designated broker, termination of that relationship requires notice to the Department, and the salesperson may not legally engage in licensed real estate activity until properly re-affiliated with another designated broker.
source_note: A.R.S. Title 32, Chapter 20, salesperson-broker affiliation and notification requirements

question: Why is it important for an Arizona licensee to clarify agency status with a customer who is browsing homes at an open house without representation?
choice_a: Because open houses automatically create a buyer agency relationship
choice_b: So the customer understands the licensee's fiduciary loyalty runs to the seller, not to them, avoiding a false assumption of representation
choice_c: Because Arizona law prohibits speaking with unrepresented buyers at all
choice_d: Because the customer must sign a listing agreement before entering the home
explanation: Clarifying agency status prevents an unrepresented visitor from mistakenly believing the seller's agent represents their interests, which is essential given that fiduciary duties like loyalty and confidentiality are owed only to the agent's actual client, the seller.
source_note: Arizona Department of Real Estate agency-disclosure best practices

question: Which of these is a proper example of the fiduciary duty of loyalty in action for an Arizona seller's agent?
choice_a: Secretly recommending the seller's home to a family member at a reduced price without disclosure
choice_b: Accepting an undisclosed bonus from a title company for steering the seller's business there
choice_c: Declining to represent a buyer making an offer on the same listed property, to avoid a conflict of interest, unless proper dual/designated agency consent is obtained
choice_d: Failing to mention a competing, higher offer to the seller
explanation: Loyalty requires the agent to avoid conflicts of interest and self-dealing. Recognizing a potential conflict when representing both sides and taking the proper procedural step (obtaining consent for dual/designated agency, or declining) reflects genuine loyalty to the client's interests, unlike self-dealing or undisclosed incentives.
source_note: Arizona fiduciary duty of loyalty (OLDCAR framework)

question: Under Arizona practice, what should a licensee do if a prospective client asks the licensee to represent them, but the licensee's designated broker already represents the other party to the same transaction under a separate agreement?
choice_a: Simply agree to represent both sides without telling either party
choice_b: Refuse to work with the client and provide no explanation
choice_c: Automatically assume dual agency is illegal and cannot proceed under any structure
choice_d: Discuss designated agency options with the broker, since the same firm may already represent the other side, and proceed only with proper disclosure and consent as required
explanation: When both parties to a transaction are represented by licensees within the same firm, Arizona practice generally calls for designated agency (separate representation) or properly consented dual agency, with full disclosure to both parties before proceeding, rather than either silently representing both or refusing to help at all.
source_note: Arizona Department of Real Estate designated agency and dual agency disclosure requirements

question: Which of the following most accurately reflects the scope of the Arizona Broker exam's testing on 'Brokerage Business' within the Agency Relationships and Managerial Duties content area?
choice_a: The designated/employing broker's supervisory relationship over affiliated salespersons and associate brokers
choice_b: Only the mechanics of preparing marketing flyers
choice_c: Only federal income tax treatment of commission income
choice_d: Only how to price a home using comparable sales
explanation: The Brokerage Business content area centers on the designated (employing) broker's supervisory role and responsibilities over the salespersons and associate brokers within the firm, reflecting Arizona's real broker-supervision structure under statute.
source_note: Pearson VUE Arizona Real Estate Broker Candidate Handbook and Content Outline (Feb. 2026)

question: An Arizona buyer's agent discovers, through the transaction, a serious latent structural defect in the home the buyer is purchasing. What does the fiduciary duty of disclosure require of the agent toward their own buyer-client?
choice_a: The agent may withhold it if disclosure could delay closing
choice_b: The agent must promptly inform the buyer-client of the material information
choice_c: The agent should only disclose it if the buyer specifically asks about structural issues
choice_d: Disclosure to the client is optional once the purchase contract is signed
explanation: The duty of disclosure obligates an agent to promptly share material information relevant to the transaction with their own client, including problems discovered about the property, regardless of whether the client specifically asked or whether it may complicate closing.
source_note: Arizona fiduciary duty of disclosure (OLDCAR framework)

question: How does an Arizona buyer-broker agreement typically address the broker's compensation if the seller's listing agreement already offers cooperating compensation to a buyer's broker?
choice_a: The buyer's broker is legally barred from accepting any compensation from the seller's side
choice_b: The buyer must always pay the broker in cash outside of closing, with no reference to seller-offered compensation
choice_c: The agreement can specify how any seller-offered compensation will be credited or coordinated with the buyer's obligation to the buyer's broker
choice_d: Compensation terms may never be included in a buyer-broker agreement
explanation: A properly drafted Arizona buyer-broker agreement addresses how the broker will be compensated, including how any compensation offered by the seller's side will be applied toward or coordinated with what the buyer has agreed to pay, providing clarity and avoiding double payment.
source_note: Arizona Department of Real Estate buyer representation agreement content requirements

question: A designated broker in Arizona delegates day-to-day supervisory duties for one branch office to another qualified broker. Does this delegation eliminate the designated broker's ultimate responsibility for that branch?
choice_a: Yes -- delegation completely transfers all legal responsibility away from the designated broker
choice_b: Delegation is not permitted under any circumstances in Arizona
choice_c: Delegation converts the branch into an entirely separate, unlicensed entity
choice_d: No -- the designated broker remains ultimately accountable to the Department even when supervisory tasks are delegated
explanation: While a designated broker may delegate supervisory tasks to another qualified licensee for practical office management, the designated broker retains ultimate statutory responsibility and accountability to the Arizona Department of Real Estate for the brokerage's overall compliance.
source_note: A.R.S. Title 32, Chapter 20, designated broker ultimate accountability framework

question: What is the main reason Arizona requires an agency-relationship disclosure to be made to all parties, not just the licensee's own client?
choice_a: So that unrepresented or differently represented parties understand what duties, if any, the licensee owes them before sharing information or relying on the licensee's advice
choice_b: Because non-clients are legally entitled to the same fiduciary duties as clients
choice_c: Because it eliminates the need for a written listing agreement
choice_d: Because it allows licensees to avoid ever disclosing material facts
explanation: Agency disclosure protects consumers by making clear, before they share sensitive information or rely on advice, exactly whose interests the licensee represents and what level of duty (fiduciary vs. basic honesty and fair dealing) applies to them.
source_note: Arizona Department of Real Estate agency-disclosure consumer protection rationale

question: Which of the following would be considered a properly documented termination of an Arizona listing agreement before its stated expiration date?
choice_a: The seller simply stops returning the agent's calls
choice_b: A written mutual release signed by both the seller and the broker
choice_c: The seller lists the property with another broker without informing the first broker
choice_d: The agreement automatically terminates the moment an offer is rejected
explanation: Because a listing agreement is a binding contract for its stated term, early termination generally requires a written mutual release or agreement between broker and seller, rather than informal abandonment or the seller unilaterally engaging a second broker.
source_note: General Arizona listing agreement contract practice

question: Which of the following best distinguishes a general agent from a special (limited) agent in real estate agency law, as applied to a typical Arizona listing arrangement?
choice_a: A general agent may only act in a single transaction
choice_b: A special agent has unlimited authority to bind the principal in all matters
choice_c: A special agent, like a typical listing broker, is authorized to conduct a specific, limited transaction, while a general agent has broader ongoing authority to act for the principal across multiple matters
choice_d: There is no meaningful distinction between the two in agency law
explanation: A real estate listing broker is typically a special (limited) agent, authorized to perform a specific task (marketing and selling one property) rather than a general agent with broad, ongoing authority to act for the principal in many matters, such as a property manager might have.
source_note: General agency law classifications applied to Arizona real estate brokerage

question: An Arizona property manager who is authorized to handle rent collection, maintenance contracts, and tenant relations on an ongoing basis for an owner is typically classified as what kind of agent?
choice_a: A special agent limited to one transaction
choice_b: A subagent of the tenant only
choice_c: A dual agent by default
choice_d: A general agent
explanation: Because a property manager is authorized to handle a range of ongoing matters for the owner rather than a single, discrete transaction, this arrangement is typically classified as general agency, contrasted with the special (limited) agency of a typical one-property listing broker.
source_note: General agency law classifications applied to Arizona property management

question: Under Arizona practice, what should a designated broker do upon learning that a salesperson in the firm may have violated a fiduciary duty owed to a client?
choice_a: Investigate and take appropriate corrective or disciplinary action, since the broker bears supervisory responsibility for the firm's licensees
choice_b: Ignore it unless the client files a lawsuit
choice_c: Immediately terminate the salesperson's license permanently without any Department involvement
choice_d: Report only to the salesperson's family members
explanation: Because the designated broker bears supervisory responsibility and can be disciplined for failing to reasonably supervise licensees, appropriate practice requires the broker to investigate suspected fiduciary violations and take corrective action, which may also involve reporting to the Arizona Department of Real Estate depending on severity.
source_note: A.R.S. Section 32-2153, designated broker supervisory and disciplinary responsibility

question: In a limited representation (transaction broker) role recognized in Arizona practice, which duties still apply even though full fiduciary duties do not?
choice_a: Full loyalty and confidentiality identical to single agency
choice_b: Honesty, fair dealing, and disclosure of material facts to both parties
choice_c: No duties whatsoever apply
choice_d: Only a duty to close the transaction as quickly as possible
explanation: Even without a full fiduciary agency relationship, a transaction broker or limited representative still owes baseline duties of honesty, fair dealing, and disclosure of known material facts to the parties involved, distinguishing limited representation from having no duties at all.
source_note: Arizona Department of Real Estate limited representation/transaction broker duties framework

question: Which best describes the relationship between an Arizona designated broker and the brokerage entity (such as an LLC or corporation) under which real estate business is conducted?
choice_a: The brokerage entity itself is personally licensed and takes on all liability, with no individual designated broker required
choice_b: Any officer of the entity, licensed or not, may serve as designated broker
choice_c: The designated broker is the licensed individual legally responsible for the entity's real estate license and its licensees' compliance with real estate law
choice_d: A designated broker is optional if the entity carries sufficient insurance
explanation: Arizona requires a real estate brokerage entity to have a qualifying, individually licensed designated broker who bears personal, statutory responsibility for the entity's compliance and the supervision of its licensees; an unlicensed officer cannot fill that role.
source_note: A.R.S. Title 32, Chapter 20, designated broker requirement for licensed entities

question: A seller instructs their Arizona listing agent, in writing, not to disclose a recent professional pest inspection report showing termite damage to potential buyers. What should the agent do?
choice_a: Follow the seller's instruction without question because of the duty of obedience
choice_b: Disclose it only to the Arizona Department of Real Estate and no one else
choice_c: Immediately terminate the listing agreement without discussing the issue with the seller
choice_d: Advise the seller that material fact disclosure obligations under Arizona law and honesty duties to the buyer-customer may still require disclosure, and decline to follow an instruction that could facilitate concealment of a material defect
explanation: The duty of obedience only extends to lawful instructions. An instruction to conceal a known material defect from a buyer could violate Arizona disclosure law and consumer protection principles, so the agent should not blindly follow it and should counsel the seller on the legal risk instead.
source_note: Arizona fiduciary duty of obedience limited by legal disclosure obligations; general Arizona seller disclosure practice

question: What is the practical significance of Arizona requiring 'informed' consent (not just any consent) for dual agency?
choice_a: The parties must actually understand the tradeoffs and limitations of dual agency, such as reduced undivided loyalty, before agreeing to it
choice_b: It means the broker, not the client, decides whether consent is valid
choice_c: It removes any requirement that consent be in writing
choice_d: It has no practical difference from ordinary consent
explanation: Requiring 'informed' consent means the client must genuinely understand what dual agency entails -- including that full, undivided loyalty is no longer possible -- before agreeing, which is a stronger protection than a client simply signing a form without understanding its implications.
source_note: Arizona Department of Real Estate dual agency informed-consent standard

question: Which of the following would most likely NOT be found in a properly drafted Arizona exclusive listing agreement?
choice_a: The listing price and property description
choice_b: A clause guaranteeing the broker will find a buyer within seven days or forfeit all rights to any commission
choice_c: The agreed commission rate or fee structure
choice_d: A specific termination date
explanation: Real, standard Arizona listing agreements include the price, description, commission terms, and a definite termination date, but they do not typically include an unrealistic guarantee like finding a buyer within seven days or forfeiting the commission -- that is not a standard or required element and misrepresents how brokerage services work.
source_note: Arizona Department of Real Estate listing agreement required-content standards

question: How does Arizona's designated agency model attempt to solve the divided-loyalty problem inherent in dual agency?
choice_a: By eliminating fiduciary duties for both parties entirely
choice_b: By requiring both parties to use the exact same individual licensee
choice_c: By assigning each party their own individual agent within the firm who owes that party full, undivided fiduciary duties, while the designated broker oversees both
choice_d: By transferring all fiduciary duties to the escrow company
explanation: Designated agency solves the divided-loyalty issue of dual agency by giving each party their own designated licensee within the firm, each owing full, undivided fiduciary duties to their respective client, while the designated broker retains overall supervisory responsibility.
source_note: Arizona Department of Real Estate designated agency structural framework

question: Which of these situations would require an Arizona licensee to make a fresh, updated agency disclosure to a party already met earlier in a different transaction?
choice_a: The party already received a disclosure once, so no further disclosure is ever needed for that person again
choice_b: Agency disclosure is a one-time, lifetime requirement not tied to specific transactions
choice_c: Disclosure is required only if the party specifically requests it
choice_d: The licensee is beginning a brand-new transaction with that same party where the agency relationship or role may differ from before
explanation: Agency disclosure is transaction-specific; because the licensee's role (representing the seller, the buyer, both, or neither) can differ from one transaction to the next, a new, accurate disclosure should be made at the outset of each new transaction rather than relying on an old one.
source_note: Arizona Department of Real Estate agency-disclosure, transaction-specific application

question: A designated broker in Arizona personally lists and sells very few properties but spends most work hours training, auditing files, and reviewing contracts for the firm's fifteen salespersons. Which managerial duty is being fulfilled here?
choice_a: The statutory duty to exercise reasonable supervision over affiliated licensees
choice_b: The fiduciary duty of loyalty owed directly to a specific buyer
choice_c: The duty of confidentiality owed to a specific seller
choice_d: A duty owed only under federal Fair Housing law
explanation: Training, auditing transaction files, and reviewing contracts across the firm are hallmark activities of the designated broker's statutory duty to reasonably supervise the licensees under their responsibility, distinct from an individual fiduciary duty owed within a single transaction.
source_note: A.R.S. Section 32-2155, designated broker supervisory duty in practice

question: Under A.A.C. R4-28-1101(C), what must an Arizona licensee do if the licensee is unable to perform an act required by rule or statute?
choice_a: Wait until the next license renewal cycle to disclose the issue
choice_b: Expeditiously notify their designated broker of the inability to perform
choice_c: Notify only the client, since the designated broker has no role in individual transactions
choice_d: Do nothing further, as long as the client is not ultimately harmed
explanation: R4-28-1101(C) requires a licensee to expeditiously perform all acts required by holding a license, without intentional or neglectful delay, and if the licensee is unable to perform such an act, to promptly notify the designated broker of that inability.
source_note: A.A.C. R4-28-1101(C) (Licensee Duties)

question: Two Arizona licensees on opposite sides of a transaction have a personal dispute over an unrelated matter. Under A.A.C. R4-28-1101(D), what does this rule require regarding the current transaction?
choice_a: Both licensees must immediately terminate their agency relationships with their respective clients
choice_b: Both licensees must report each other to the Department before any further work on the file
choice_c: Neither licensee may allow the controversy with the other licensee to jeopardize, delay, or interfere with initiating, processing, or finalizing the transaction on behalf of their clients
choice_d: The transaction may be freely delayed until the personal dispute between the licensees is resolved
explanation: R4-28-1101(D) prohibits a licensee from allowing a controversy with another licensee to jeopardize, delay, or interfere with the initiation, processing, or finalizing of a transaction being handled on behalf of a client.
source_note: A.A.C. R4-28-1101(D) (Licensee Duties)

question: Under A.A.C. R4-28-1101(D), the rule against letting a controversy with another licensee interfere with a transaction does NOT obligate a licensee to do which of the following?
choice_a: Continue processing the transaction toward closing in good faith
choice_b: Deal fairly with all other parties to the transaction
choice_c: Perform license-required acts without unreasonable delay
choice_d: Agree to alter the terms of an employment or compensation agreement, or relinquish the right to maintain an action to resolve the controversy
explanation: R4-28-1101(D) expressly clarifies that the prohibition on letting a controversy interfere with a transaction does not force a licensee to alter the terms of an employment or compensation agreement, nor to give up the right to pursue legal action to resolve the controversy.
source_note: A.A.C. R4-28-1101(D) (Licensee Duties)

question: Under A.A.C. R4-28-1101(E)(2), a licensee must disclose in writing, before a binding agreement is entered, if the purchaser or seller is a member of whose immediate family?
choice_a: The licensee's immediate family, or the licensee's designated broker's immediate family
choice_b: Only the licensee's own immediate family, never the designated broker's
choice_c: Only the immediate family of the buyer's lender
choice_d: Only the immediate family of the escrow officer handling the closing
explanation: R4-28-1101(E)(2) requires written pre-agreement disclosure when the purchaser or seller is a member of either the licensee's immediate family or the licensee's designated broker's immediate family, not just the licensee's own relatives.
source_note: A.A.C. R4-28-1101(E)(2) (Licensee Duties)

question: Under A.A.C. R4-28-1101(E)(3), written disclosure before a binding agreement is required if the purchaser or seller has what relationship to the licensee's employing broker?
choice_a: A prior unrelated real estate transaction with the employing broker more than five years earlier
choice_b: Ownership in, or is an employee of, the licensee's employing broker
choice_c: A personal social media connection with the employing broker
choice_d: No relationship of this kind triggers a disclosure obligation under Arizona rule
explanation: R4-28-1101(E)(3) requires written disclosure, before the parties enter a binding agreement, when the purchaser or seller has ownership in, or is an employee of, the licensee's employing broker.
source_note: A.A.C. R4-28-1101(E)(3) (Licensee Duties)

question: Under A.A.C. R4-28-1101(E)(4), written disclosure before a binding agreement is required if the licensee or an immediate family member has what kind of interest in the transaction?
choice_a: Any interest at all, including merely knowing the buyer socially
choice_b: A financial interest, but only if it exceeds $10,000 in value
choice_c: A financial interest in the transaction other than the licensee's receipt of compensation for real estate services
choice_d: No such disclosure is ever required if the interest is indirect
explanation: R4-28-1101(E)(4) requires written disclosure of a present or prospective financial interest that the licensee, or a member of the licensee's immediate family, has in the transaction, beyond the licensee's ordinary compensation for real estate services.
source_note: A.A.C. R4-28-1101(E)(4) (Licensee Duties)

question: Under A.A.C. R4-28-1101(G), a licensee generally may not accept compensation or a rebate for goods or services related to a real estate transaction without what safeguard, and what is the key exception?
choice_a: No safeguard is required as long as the amount is under $500
choice_b: Verbal acknowledgement is sufficient, and there is no exception for broker-to-broker payments
choice_c: The compensation must instead be donated to a charitable organization rather than accepted
choice_d: The person's prior written acknowledgement of the compensation is required, except this does not apply to compensation paid to a broker by another broker representing a party in the transaction
explanation: R4-28-1101(G) requires a person's prior written acknowledgement before a licensee accepts compensation or a rebate tied to related goods or services, but this prohibition does not apply to compensation paid to a broker by another broker who represents a party in the transaction.
source_note: A.A.C. R4-28-1101(G) (Licensee Duties)

question: Under A.A.C. R4-28-1101(H), if a matter falls outside a licensee's field of competence, what must occur before the licensee may proceed personally rather than engaging a competent third party?
choice_a: The licensee's lack of expertise must first be disclosed to the client in writing, and the client must subsequently employ the licensee anyway
choice_b: The licensee may proceed without disclosure as long as the client never asks about qualifications
choice_c: The Department must first issue a temporary competence waiver
choice_d: The licensee must complete a specific continuing education course within 30 days after the transaction closes
explanation: R4-28-1101(H) requires that services conform to recognized standards of competence, and if a licensee lacks expertise in a given discipline, the licensee must either engage someone competent or first disclose that lack of expertise to the client in writing, with the client then choosing to employ the licensee anyway.
source_note: A.A.C. R4-28-1101(H) (Licensee Duties)

question: Under A.A.C. R4-28-1101(I), the duty of reasonable care requires an Arizona licensee to do what regarding information relevant to a client's transaction?
choice_a: Independently verify every fact using a licensed inspector at the licensee's own personal expense
choice_b: Obtain material information relevant to the contemplated transaction, accurately communicate it to the client, and take reasonable steps to help the client confirm its accuracy
choice_c: Rely solely on information supplied by the opposing party's agent without independent evaluation
choice_d: Communicate only the information that supports the client's preferred outcome in the transaction
explanation: R4-28-1101(I) requires a licensee to exercise reasonable care in obtaining information material to the client's interests, to accurately communicate that information to the client, and to take reasonable steps to help the client confirm its accuracy.
source_note: A.A.C. R4-28-1101(I) (Licensee Duties)

question: Under A.A.C. R4-28-1101(J)(1), a licensee may not permit or facilitate access to or occupancy in a person's real property without what?
choice_a: Verbal permission from any licensee involved in the transaction
choice_b: A pending purchase contract, regardless of the owner's wishes
choice_c: Prior written authorization from the owner of the real property
choice_d: Approval from the buyer's lender only
explanation: R4-28-1101(J)(1) prohibits a licensee from permitting or facilitating access to, or occupancy in, a person's real property without prior written authorization from the property's owner.
source_note: A.A.C. R4-28-1101(J)(1) (Licensee Duties)

question: Under A.A.C. R4-28-1101(K), an Arizona licensee must recommend that a client seek appropriate counsel from which professionals regarding the risks of pre-possession or post-possession of a property?
choice_a: Only a structural engineer
choice_b: Only the licensee's own designated broker
choice_c: No recommendation is required if the client is an experienced investor
choice_d: Insurance, legal, tax, and accounting professionals
explanation: R4-28-1101(K) requires a licensee to recommend that the client seek appropriate counsel from insurance, legal, tax, and accounting professionals regarding the risks associated with pre-possession or post-possession of a property.
source_note: A.A.C. R4-28-1101(K) (Licensee Duties)

question: Under A.A.C. R4-28-1102(B), unless the buyer waives the requirement in writing, negotiations on the buyer's behalf must be conducted exclusively through whom?
choice_a: The buyer's principal broker or the broker's representative, unless the designated broker, a broker with delegated authority, and the buyer's licensee are all unavailable for 24 hours
choice_b: Any licensee at any brokerage who happens to be available at the time
choice_c: The seller's designated broker directly, bypassing the buyer's own broker entirely
choice_d: The title company handling escrow for the transaction
explanation: R4-28-1102(B) requires that, unless the buyer waives the requirement in writing, negotiations be conducted exclusively through the buyer's principal broker or the broker's representative, with a narrow exception when the designated broker, a broker with delegated authority, and the buyer's own licensee are all unavailable for 24 hours.
source_note: A.A.C. R4-28-1102(B) (Property Negotiations)

question: Under A.A.C. R4-28-1103(B), the compliance-monitoring system a designated broker must establish is required to include what specific element?
choice_a: A mandatory annual bonus structure for the firm's top-producing licensees
choice_b: A progressive disciplinary policy for managing violations of the employing broker's policies that would also violate a statutory requirement or prohibition related to real estate activity
choice_c: A requirement that all affiliated licensees use the same third-party marketing vendor
choice_d: A policy allowing licensees to opt out of supervision after five years of licensed experience
explanation: R4-28-1103(B) requires the designated broker's compliance-monitoring system to include, at minimum, a progressive disciplinary policy addressing violations of the employing broker's own policies that would also constitute a statutory violation, and failing to enforce that disciplinary policy is itself a violation of subsection (D).
source_note: A.A.C. R4-28-1103(B) (Broker Supervision and Control)

question: Under A.A.C. R4-28-1103(C), a designated broker's supervisory duty extends not only to supervising licensees and employees but also to what?
choice_a: Supervising licensees affiliated with every other brokerage located in the same city
choice_b: Supervising only unlicensed clerical staff, and not any licensed personnel
choice_c: Exercising reasonable supervision and control over the designated broker's own activities for which a license is required
choice_d: Nothing further -- the duty under this subsection is limited strictly to other licensees
explanation: R4-28-1103(C) requires a designated broker to supervise the licensees and employees of the employing broker, and also to exercise reasonable supervision and control over the designated broker's own activities for which a license is required.
source_note: A.A.C. R4-28-1103(C) (Broker Supervision and Control)

question: Under A.A.C. R4-28-1103(E), if a designated broker uses employees to help administer supervisory functions, what remains true?
choice_a: The designated broker is fully relieved of supervisory responsibility once the tasks are delegated
choice_b: The assisting employees assume personal licensure responsibility equivalent to the designated broker's
choice_c: The Department automatically transfers the designated broker's license to the delegated employee
choice_d: The designated broker may not relinquish overall responsibility for supervision and control of the employing broker's employees
explanation: R4-28-1103(E) allows a designated broker to use the services of employees to help administer supervisory provisions, but expressly provides that the designated broker may not relinquish overall responsibility for supervision and control of the employing broker's employees.
source_note: A.A.C. R4-28-1103(E) (Broker Supervision and Control)
